headline: Whales Win: Global Ban on Commercial Hunting Survives Challenge
meta_description: A controversial push to revive commercial whaling failed at the International Whaling Commission's biennial meeting in Tasmania, keeping a 40-year-old moratori…
summary_short: At its 70th meeting in Hobart, the International Whaling Commission rejected a bid to reopen commercial whaling, preserving four decades of protection for vulnerable cet…
body:
At the International Whaling Commission's 70th meeting in Hobart, Tasmania, a last-minute attempt to pave the way for commercial whaling collapsed when Grenada withdrew a controversial resolution on the final day. The draft, introduced by Antigua and Barbuda and co-sponsored by four other nations, had sought to reopen discussion of "sustainable use of whale resources"—a rhetorical gateway toward resuming hunts that have been banned globally for 40 years. The withdrawal preserved one of conservation's most celebrated victories: the 1986 moratorium that halted the industrial-scale slaughter that once pushed multiple whale species toward extinction. About 400 delegates from 89 member governments gathered for the September-October meeting, which also marked the IWC's 80th anniversary.

The resolution's sponsors received backing from Japan, which withdrew from the IWC in 2019 but remains influential as an observer, along with Norway and Iceland, which still conduct commercial hunts under legal exemptions. Observers noted that some pro-whaling votes came from nations with no whaling history—a pattern critics say reflects geopolitical pressure and aid dependency rather than genuine maritime interests. Yet the majority held firm. As one conservation leader noted, the IWC's steadfastness on the ban represents "one of the most shining success stories in global wildlife protection."

The meeting revealed both progress and unfinished work. Delegates approved new resolutions addressing whale strandings, vessel strikes, and the fish maw trade. However, a proposal for a South Atlantic Whale Sanctuary failed once more—blocked by a handful of dissenting nations despite receiving substantial support. Scientists remain concerned about threats that weren't fully addressed: climate change is disrupting cetacean food supplies and migration patterns, while one in four cetacean species now face extinction risk. The battle to protect whales continues on multiple fronts.
quick_facts: 70th IWC meeting held in Hobart, Tasmania in late September 2024
40-year-old commercial whaling ban remained intact after resolution withdrawn
One in four cetacean species currently threatened with extinction
Japan, Norway, and Iceland continue commercial whaling despite the moratorium
South Atlantic Whale Sanctuary proposal blocked again by minority of nations
